title: Higher metformin levels in heart failure: decreased renal blood flow (reduced clearance)
vignette: Researchers investigating the effects of heart failure on the pharmacokinetics of antidiabetic medications develop a cohort of experimental animals with anthracycline-induced heart failure. The experimental animals are then administered an oral dose of metformin, and serum levels are monitored over time. The test is repeated in control animals with normal heart function, and the results are shown below: the experimental (heart failure) group shows higher and more prolonged serum metformin concentrations than the control group. Which of the following best explains the change in serum metformin levels seen in the experimental animals?

clues.note: Anthracyclines (e.g., doxorubicin) cause dilated cardiomyopathy; heart failure lowers cardiac output and organ perfusion, altering drug handling.
Metformin is NOT metabolized by the liver; it is eliminated UNCHANGED by the kidneys, so its clearance depends on renal perfusion/function.

clues.text: higher and more prolonged serum metformin concentrations
clues.note: Elevated, prolonged levels indicate REDUCED clearance - in heart failure this is due to decreased renal blood flow from low cardiac output.

whatMatters: METFORMIN is cleared UNCHANGED by the KIDNEYS. Heart failure lowers cardiac output and thus RENAL BLOOD FLOW, reducing metformin's renal clearance -> higher and more prolonged serum levels (and increased lactic-acidosis risk). Answer B.
strategy: Anchor on metformin's elimination: renal (unchanged), not hepatic. Reduced cardiac output in HF -> decreased renal perfusion -> decreased clearance -> higher levels. Reject CYP inhibition and hepatic congestion (metformin isn't hepatically metabolized), extracellular fluid accumulation (increased Vd would DECREASE peak levels, not raise them), and intestinal wall edema (would REDUCE/delay absorption -> lower levels).

eliminations.label: CYP inhibition - metformin isn't CYP-metabolized
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: reduced hepatic CYP metabolism raising drug levels. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: metformin is excreted UNCHANGED by the kidney and is not metabolized by CYP enzymes, so CYP inhibition wouldn't change its levels. ✅ Correct if: a CYP-metabolized drug accumulating from enzyme inhibition.

eliminations.label: Extracellular fluid accumulation - would lower peak levels
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: expanded volume of distribution from edema. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a larger Vd would DILUTE the drug and DECREASE serum concentration, not raise it. ✅ Correct if: explaining a lower peak concentration of a water-soluble drug.

eliminations.label: Hepatic venous congestion - metformin isn't hepatically cleared
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: reduced hepatic drug metabolism from congestion/hypoperfusion. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: metformin is not metabolized by the liver; its clearance is renal, so hepatic congestion doesn't explain the rise. ✅ Correct if: a hepatically metabolized drug accumulating in congestive hepatopathy.

eliminations.label: Intestinal wall edema - would reduce absorption
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: gut wall edema impairing oral absorption. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: reduced/delayed absorption would LOWER serum levels, opposite to the observed increase. ✅ Correct if: decreased/delayed peak from impaired oral absorption.

reasoning: Metformin is eliminated unchanged by the kidneys (not metabolized)
Heart failure reduces cardiac output and therefore renal blood flow
Decreased renal perfusion lowers metformin clearance
-> higher, prolonged serum levels; answer B
mechanism: HEART FAILURE alters pharmacokinetics chiefly by reducing CARDIAC OUTPUT, which lowers perfusion of the organs responsible for drug clearance. METFORMIN is a hydrophilic drug that is NOT metabolized; it is eliminated UNCHANGED by the KIDNEYS (via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion). When cardiac output falls, RENAL BLOOD FLOW decreases, reducing metformin's renal clearance and prolonging its elimination - producing the HIGHER and more sustained serum concentrations seen in the heart-failure animals. Clinically this matters because reduced clearance raises the risk of LACTIC ACIDOSIS, so metformin is used cautiously in patients with heart failure or renal impairment. The distractors don't fit metformin's handling: it isn't CYP-metabolized (so CYP inhibition/hepatic congestion are irrelevant), an expanded volume of distribution (edema) would lower rather than raise levels, and intestinal wall edema would impair absorption and reduce levels.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm > metformin: renally excreted unchanged; caution in renal impairment/heart failure (lactic acidosis); heart failure lowers cardiac output -> reduced hepatic/renal perfusion -> reduced clearance of renally/hepatically cleared drugs.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Metformin is renally cleared; HF drops renal blood flow -> less clearance -> higher levels.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on renal clearance, cardiac output, volume of distribution, metformin elimination, or lactic acidosis? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: CYP/hepatic congestion don't apply (not hepatically metabolized); edema increases Vd (lowers levels); gut edema lowers absorption.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: Concentration-time graph (stem): the heart-failure curve is higher and decays more slowly than control = reduced clearance -> decreased renal blood flow.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: metformin renally cleared; heart failure -> decreased renal blood flow -> higher levels -> lactic acidosis risk.

keywords.back: Low cardiac output -> reduced renal/hepatic perfusion -> reduced clearance

memoryHook: Metformin leaves only through the kidneys; a failing heart starves the kidneys of blood, so the drug lingers and piles up (watch for lactic acidosis).
